sources.title: Ahmad Amin (Q2762564), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-06): English label 'Ahmad Amin', no Korean label, description 'Egyptian historian and writer (1886-1954)', born 1 October 1886, died 29 May 1954, citizenship Egypt, image 'Ahmad Amin Portrait.jpg'. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Hulusi Kilic, 'Ahmed Emin', TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (Turkish Diyanet Foundation Encyclopaedia of Islam, vol. 2, 1989; online edition, read in full in Turkish). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Egyptian scholar born in Cairo, schooled at al-Azhar and the Madrasat al-Qada al-Shar'i, taught, served as a judge for four years, joined Cairo University's Faculty of Arts in 1926 through Taha Husayn, divided the work on Islamic intellectual history with Taha Husayn and Abd al-Hamid al-Abbadi, which produced the Fajr al-Islam series (Fajr al-Islam 1928, Duha al-Islam 1933-36, Zuhr al-Islam 1945-55, an analytical and critical survey of Islamic culture to the 4th/10th century), became dean of the Faculty of Arts in 1939, director of cultural affairs of the Arab League in 1947, presided throughout his life over the Committee for Authorship, Translation and Publication that he had founded with friends in 1914, wrote in al-Risala and al-Thaqafa, collected about 700 articles in the ten-volume Fayd al-Khatir, and with colleagues prepared some twenty school textbooks and scholarly editions of Arabic classics between 1926 and 1954. States that Western methods and orientalist influence (Brockelmann in particular) marked his work, that he was not popular in Islamic circles and that his views on hadith, Quran commentary and Arabic literary history were criticised by named scholars, including twenty-two articles by Zaki Mubarak in al-Risala in 1939. Reference work; the encyclopedia is written from a traditional religious-studies standpoint, so its critical passages are a counter-voice rather than neutral assessment.

Adnan Demircan, 'Ahmed Emin (Hayati, Eserleri ve Bazi Gorusleri)' [Ahmad Amin: his life, works and some views], Dogu Arastirmalari 1 (2008), pp. 101-ff. (open-access PDF, read in the life and works sections in Turkish). A scholarly biography built mainly on Amin's autobiography Hayati and on al-Zirikli's Al-A'lam: his teaching and lecturing post at the Madrasat al-Qada, learning English from British women, the Committee founded in 1914 which he headed until 1953, his move to a judge's post after a dispute following the dismissal of his dean, his 1926 appointment to the Faculty of Letters on Taha Husayn's proposal, library research in Istanbul in 1928, heading faculty study trips to Syria and Iraq, election to the 1932 Orientalists' Congress in Leiden, the 1939 deanship which he left in its second year after a disagreement with the Minister of Education, the 1945 People's University set up with two friends, and the lists of his works and textbooks. The biography is largely a paraphrase of the subject's own memoir, so it is not independent of it; the work-lists are independent.

Betul Oz, 'Misirli Mutefekkir Ahmed Emin'in (ol. 1954) Hadis Anlayisinin Tespiti ve Degerlendirilmesi' [Determination and evaluation of the hadith understanding of the Egyptian thinker Ahmad Amin], Uludag Universitesi Ilahiyat Fakultesi Dergisi 31(1), 2022, pp. 265-299 (open-access PDF; introduction, conclusion and the sections on his hadith criticism read in Turkish). A specialist critique from a faculty of theology: summarises his career (teacher, qadi, professor and dean, the two-year study that produced Fajr al-Islam in 1928, about two more years for Duha al-Islam, the pause in writing while he was dean and the completion of Zuhr al-Islam after he resigned), says he followed orientalist writers such as Goldziher, Nallino and Brockelmann, and argues that he did not study the primary sources of hadith criticism, quoted Bukhari hadiths through commentaries and legal-theory works rather than the original source, and adopted orientalist views without analysis. COUNTER-VOICE for the sources above. The life facts again come from Hayati; the criticism is a traditionalist hadith scholar's and concerns only the hadith chapters.

Ahmad Amin, 'Hayati' [My Life], first published Cairo: Committee for Authorship, Translation and Publication, 1950 (OpenITI digital text of the Hindawi edition on the Internet Archive, item wuquf-openiti-1373ahmadamin.hayati-721889315c33; Arabic; the passages on the Committee, his work routine, his working life after retirement and the offers of editorship read in Arabic). SELF-REPORT: an autobiography written by the subject, used only for documented episodes and his own account of his working habits, never as the sole support for a row; the whole book was not read.

collaboration.rationale: [src_amin_tdv, src_amin_demircan2008 | 1914-1954 | encyclopedia, scholarly biography] The encyclopedia records that he founded the Committee for Authorship, Translation and Publication with friends in 1914 and presided over it for life, that he agreed a division of labour on Islamic cultural history with Taha Husayn and Abd al-Hamid al-Abbadi (his part became the Fajr al-Islam series), that he prepared about twenty school textbooks with Taha Husayn and other colleagues between 1926 and 1954 and co-edited Arabic classics with named colleagues; Demircan independently lists the co-written works and says he headed the Committee until 1953. Two sources and the co-authored editions agree; the dates of his role differ slightly (founded vs. appointed head), so confidence stays at 0.55.

discipline.rationale: [src_amin_tdv, src_amin_demircan2008, src_amin_hayati1950 | 1920-1954 | encyclopedia, scholarly biography, memoir] The documented output is large and sustained: the eight-volume Fajr, Duha and Zuhr al-Islam series (1928-1955), about 700 articles collected in ten volumes of Fayd al-Khatir, textbooks and scholarly editions (TDV; Demircan's lists). In Hayati he describes reading in the evening and writing in the morning, working in silence and not wasting time in cafes. The output is independently listed; the routine is self-report, so the row rests on the output.

persistence.rationale: [src_amin_tdv, src_amin_oz2022, src_amin_demircan2008 | 1928-1955 | encyclopedia, hadith-studies article, scholarly biography] He carried one history project across more than a quarter of a century: Fajr al-Islam (1928) after two years of work, Duha al-Islam after about two more, a pause in writing while he was dean (1939 onwards), and Zuhr al-Islam completed after he resigned and published 1945-55 (Oz, drawing on Hayati; TDV for the publication dates), despite sharp published criticism of his earlier volumes (TDV names Zaki Mubarak's twenty-two articles of 1939). The time span and volumes are documented; the personal-effort reading is an inference.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_amin_demircan2008, src_amin_oz2022, src_amin_tdv | 1907-1932 | scholarly biography, hadith-studies article, encyclopedia] While working he took English lessons from British women (a second, better-educated teacher after the first seemed inadequate), attended orientalists' lectures, learned research methods from orientalist colleagues at the university, spent about two years on Fajr al-Islam, made a 40-day library research trip to Istanbul in 1928 and went to the 1932 Orientalists' Congress in Leiden (Demircan, Oz); TDV says he adopted Western critical method through colleagues. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.52 to 64 / 0.46 because the specific learning episodes (English lessons, lectures, trips) all trace to his own autobiography via the two articles, which footnote Hayati; only the output is independently listed.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_amin_demircan2008, src_amin_tdv | 1914-1947 | scholarly biography, encyclopedia] The activity points to educational purpose: the Committee that published Arabic classics and cultural-history works (TDV), school textbooks (TDV), and the People's University set up in 1945 with two friends, which reached 17,000 students (Demircan, citing Hayati). The activities are documented but the motive is inferred and the student figure rests on his own memoir. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.50 to 60 / 0.45 because the People's University detail is memoir-only and the motive is read from activity, not from a stated reason.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_amin_tdv, src_amin_oz2022 | 1928-1936 | encyclopedia, hadith-studies article] Both sources report that he questioned the uprightness of some Companions and the date at which hadith were first compiled, drawing published rebuttals (TDV names Sibai, Zahabi, Zaki Mubarak and others); Oz argues, however, that he largely followed orientalist views (Goldziher, Brockelmann) without examining the primary sources, so the independence of the positions is contested and the evidence comes from critics writing from a traditional standpoint. Mixed, low-confidence and dual-edged.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_amin_oz2022, src_amin_demircan2008, src_amin_tdv | 1928-1936 | hadith-studies article, scholarly biography, encyclopedia] Oz's specialist finding is that in his hadith chapters he cited Bukhari hadiths through commentaries and legal-theory works instead of the original source and reported views without testing them, and TDV records criticism of his hadith, Quran-commentary and Arabic-literary-history claims; Demircan, by contrast, describes the series as clearly written and using primary sources and orientalist studies with notes at the end of chapters. The criticisms come from traditionalist hadith scholars about one sub-field, so the row sits near the middle with low confidence.

portrait.reason: HELD. No rights-clear portrait was found after one bounded retry. The Commons images ('Ahmad Amin Portrait.jpg' 788 x 1118, 'Ahmad Amin in 1916.jpg' 955 x 1441, 'Ahmad Amin in his office in the Arab League.jpg', 'Ahmad Amin in his late days.jpg') name an unknown author, the date 'before 1955' (or 1916 without evidence of publication) and the template PD-Egypt, and their cited source is a Wikidata record for the 1955 memorial book 'Ahmad Amin in his own pen and the pen of his friends' (Cairo, 1955), not a pre-1931 publication; a jurisdiction-only public-domain tag for an unknown photographer is not a rights basis, and the date and creator are unresolved. The separate Commons file 'Ahmad Amin.jpg' cites a Hindawi contributor page whose server is behind a bot challenge, so the holder could not be checked. No photograph of him published before 1931 was found. Next step: find a dated photograph in a pre-1931 Egyptian periodical or book scan (Internet Archive or a library) with a documented publication date, or obtain a stated licence from a holder such as Cairo University, the Arab League or the family; do not use the Commons PD-Egypt files as they stand.

A web search for a pre-1931 magazine photograph found nothing. Image inscription: none checked, no image was accepted. PREFLIGHT (identity/QID/region): Wikidata Q2762564 verified live (label 'Ahmad Amin', description 'Egyptian historian and writer (1886-1954)', 1886-10-01 to 1954-05-29); no production collision (prod66.json, 762 people) and no existing candidate file or QID collision. ZERO POLITICS: scored as historian, writer, scholar, editor of cultural classics and educator only; nationalism, Arab League and ministerial posts, his dispute with ministers over his deanship, his dismissal and transfer as a judge, his refusal to edit a party newspaper and his 1940s public role are context only and are scored in no row; his religious views are scored only as documented scholarly method (hadith criticism) and criticism of it, not as belief; illness in his last years is not scored. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (lead) / CONFIRMED: dated, listed works and offices in three Turkish scholarly or reference sources, though the life detail is largely from his own autobiography. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, 'Ahmed Emin' by Hulusi Kilic (src_amin_tdv). SOURCES READ: TDV entry (full), Demircan 2008 (life and works, 16 pages), Oz 2022 (introduction, conclusion, hadith sections), Hayati 1950 (selected Arabic passages from the OpenITI text), the brief diwanalarab.com entry (not cited). PERSPECTIVES: Turkish religious-studies encyclopedia (traditionalist standpoint), a Turkish scholarly biography based on the memoir, a Turkish theology-faculty critique of his hadith views, his own memoir. Only four sources could be opened, below the six to nine target: the OpenEdition biography by Emmanuelle Perrin (Anubis bot wall), Hindawi (Cloudflare), Encyclopaedia Britannica (HTTP 403), Encyclopedia of Islam, Cragg 1955, Mazyad 1963, Boullata's 1978 translation My Life, Barak 2007 (paywalled or lending-only), AKU eCommons and the Iqbal Review article (blocked) were not opened. The four sources are not fully independent: Demircan and Oz footnote Hayati for the life, so independent behavioural support is the TDV encyclopedia and the work-lists, which caps confidence (no row above 0.55). Counter-voice: Oz and the critics named in TDV (Sibai, Zahabi, Zaki Mubarak, Halvani and others, known only through the encyclopedia). Non-self behavioural sources: TDV, Demircan (work-lists), Oz. Date notes: TDV says he founded the Committee in 1914, Demircan says he was appointed its head; Wikipedia gives 1886 birth while an article footnote mentions 1878, so no row depends on those.
